name: Ben Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Ben, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group not tied to any company, union or party. Everything's confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got three apps open on a phone clipped to the dashboard of my Yaris, which is a small hybrid I bought second-hand. Mornings I do parcel drops to the lockers along the seafront for a firm called BoxPoint, and evenings I do takeaways on whichever app is paying a bonus. I ask an AI assistant each afternoon to look at my earnings sheet and tell me which app paid best per hour last week, and it's usually right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You share a flat, you said earlier. Who with, and how does the work fit around home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: With my cousin Omar, who works at the fish market, so he's up at four and I'm in at midnight. We split a two-bed above a phone repair shop for £700 a month. Out of season, when the tourists go, my evenings drop by half, and that's when it gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to my mates who thought robots were coming next week. Then I'd go back to arguing that delivery apps should pay holiday pay, because that's still the real issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes much, and I'm good at squeezing the apps. I've never had a week without work since I started. If the hybrid battery in my Yaris dies, that's £2,000 I don't have, and that scares me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the three apps and keep tweaking which hours I work. I'd put £25 a week aside for the battery fund, and I'd keep using my AI assistant for planning and for my tax return. Maybe I'd also do the free bike-repair course at the community centre, because the e-bike riders are always looking for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless, because nothing changing means my pay doesn't go up either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your AI assistant actually do for your tax return?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I photograph my fuel receipts and it sorts them into a sheet with the mileage. Last year I claimed £400 more in costs than the year before, just because I'd actually kept the records. Omar calls it my secretary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the quiet season out of tourist months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings go from about £70 to £35, and I lean harder on BoxPoint mornings. I've learned to save a bit in August for February. Not much, but enough to cover one month's rent.

say: He'd tell friends **robot panic** was overblown, then return to arguing for **holiday pay**.
The real issue for delivery workers is still **app pay**, not technology.
think: He's good at **juggling apps** and has never had a week without work.
His real risk is the **hybrid battery**, a £2,000 repair he can't afford.
do: Keep running **three apps** and adjusting his hours by pay rate.
Put **£25 a week** into a battery fund for the Yaris.
Take the free **bike-repair course** at the community centre for side work.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **restless** because his pay won't rise either.
S0.quote: If the hybrid battery in my Yaris dies, that's £2,000 I don't have, and that scares me more than any robot.
fieldNote: Ben feels **in control** of the apps and uses AI daily to plan and do his tax.
His thin cushion is real, but **seasonal saving** shows a habit of planning ahead.
He keeps his **progressive** focus on holiday pay even when technology fades.

steps.text: Keep switching between three apps by weekly pay per hour
Save £25 a week toward a Yaris hybrid battery
Do the free bike-repair course to fix riders' e-bikes for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains get shared, like a shorter week or public money for training. I'd post about countries that tax automation. But I'd also tell other drivers to get comfortable with the tools, not scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think there's an opening here for me. If robots spread slowly, someone has to look after the first delivery robots, charge them, unstick them from kerbs, and deal with the angry customers. I'd want to be that person before anyone else thinks of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for BoxPoint or the supermarket testing pavement robots and apply the same week. I'd do an online course on robot fleet basics in the evenings, there are free ones already. And I'd keep the apps going until something pays better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit, and nervous underneath, because excited doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if those robot jobs pay less than the apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do both for a bit and see. A wage with a contract is worth something even if it's less per hour, because out of season the apps can drop to nothing. I'd take stable over flashy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of the other drivers follow you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, like Tariq who's always asking me about the AI stuff. Others would think I'm a traitor, helping the robots. I get that, but someone's going to look after the delivery robots, and I'd rather it was one of the drivers than some stranger.

say: The **gains from AI** should be shared through a shorter week or public training money.
Drivers should get **comfortable with the tools** instead of being scared of them.
think: Slow robot spread opens a role **looking after** the first delivery robots.
He wants to grab that job **before anyone else** thinks of it.
do: Apply the same week if BoxPoint or the supermarket **tests pavement robots**.
Take a **free online course** on robot fleet basics in the evenings.
Keep the **apps running** until a robot job pays better.
feel: **Excited**, with **nervousness** underneath because excitement doesn't pay rent.
S1.quote: Someone's going to look after the delivery robots, and I'd rather it was one of the drivers than some stranger.
fieldNote: Ben is the rare driver who sees robot spread as **a job**, not just a threat.
He'd accept **lower hourly pay** for a contract that covers the quiet season.
He knows other drivers may see him as a **traitor** and accepts that.

steps.text: Apply to BoxPoint or the supermarket's pavement robot trial
Take a free online course on robot fleet basics
Keep running the three apps until a robot job pays better

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income in place before 2031, not after, and that the companies who own the robots should pay into it. I'd be loud about it online. I'd also say this one's coming whether we like it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my robot-minder idea works for maybe three years. Once AGI is here in 2028, the robots of 2031 will mostly manage themselves. That means one person might watch a hundred delivery robots from a screen, and I'm not sure I'm the one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From now, I'd get into any delivery robot trial I can, because being first is the only edge I've got. I'd use the AI to learn faster, maybe basic electronics or how to run a small repair business for robots and bikes. When AGI lands, I'd also start a petition locally for a robot tax, because I believe in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly, though I don't freeze. It's more like running toward something while the floor's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one person per hundred robots. Where does that number come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I made it up, it's just a feeling. I've seen videos of warehouses where three people watch a whole floor of machines. I'd guess it's something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Omar do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar guts and packs fish, which is hard for a robot, so maybe he lasts longer than me. But the market's buying and selling would go to AI straight away. I'd want him to learn something too, but he's stubborn.

say: A **basic income** must be in place before 2031, paid for by robot owners.
This change is coming regardless, so people should **prepare now**.
think: His **robot-minder** idea may only last about three years after 2031.
Self-managing robots could mean **one job** where there were a hundred drivers.
do: Join any **delivery robot trial** he can find, to be first in line.
Use AI to learn **basic electronics** for a small repair side business.
Start a local **petition** for a robot tax once AGI lands.
feel: **Worried**, but still moving rather than freezing.
S2.quote: The robots of 2031 will mostly manage themselves. That means one person might watch a hundred delivery robots from a screen, and I'm not sure I'm the one.
fieldNote: Ben's adaptiveness keeps him **anxious** rather than alarmed, even with two years' notice.
He admits his **one per hundred** figure is a guess from videos.
He worries for his cousin Omar's market, separating **hands-on** fish work from **trading**.

steps.text: Sign up to any local delivery robot trial
Learn basic electronics with an AI tutor in the evenings
Start a local petition for a robot tax
Repair e-bikes and small robots for cash on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair, and I'd push for a public retraining fund that drivers can actually use. I'd be part of whatever drivers' group forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a good amount for someone like me. I'd have three years of AI before the robots, and I could use those three to set up a small repair and charging business for e-bikes and robots on the seafront. It's a gamble, but I'm 27, when else would I gamble?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do a proper electronics course at the college, part-time, and keep the apps for money. I'd start fixing e-bikes for riders from Omar's garage space for £20 a job. By 2031 I'd want to be the person in town who fixes small delivery machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly, with my usual worry about rent in February sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from to start a repair business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tools and parts would be about £800, which I'd build up from the £20 jobs. I wouldn't borrow, because I've seen what that did to my dad's shop. I'd go slow and keep the apps until the repairs pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad took a loan for his phone shop right before everyone bought online, so I always keep one foot in something safe. He closed after two years and was paying it off for five.

say: Five years is enough to build a **public retraining fund** drivers can use.
think: Three years between AGI and robots is a window for a **repair business**.
At 27, this is the right age to **take a gamble**.
do: Take a part-time **electronics course** at the college.
Fix riders' **e-bikes for £20** a job from his cousin's garage.
Build up **£800 for tools** without borrowing.
feel: **Hopeful**, with the usual February **rent worry** still there.
S3.quote: My dad took a loan for his phone shop right before everyone bought online, so I always keep one foot in something safe.
fieldNote: Ben sees the **AI-to-robot gap** as a business window, not just borrowed time.
His father's failed shop makes him **refuse loans**, even while gambling on a new trade.
Five years lets him feel **hopeful**, though thin savings keep a worry under it.

steps.text: Start a part-time electronics course at the local college
Fix riders' e-bikes for £20 a job from Omar's garage
Keep the delivery apps going until repairs cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no one has an excuse, not the government and not us. I'd campaign for a fair share of what the machines make, but I'd also tell my mates to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd have time to build the repair business properly and maybe hire someone. Robots around 2039 means I'd be 40 with a decade of being the guy who fixes things. I'm almost looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electronics course and then a small business course, both part-time. I'd stop the evening takeaways after two years and run repairs full-time once it covers the rent. I'd put whatever I can into tools rather than a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. This is the one where I'm in charge of what happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're almost looking forward to it. Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the repair work gets automated too, eventually. Nothing's safe forever. But with ten years, I'd have learned how to learn, and that's worth more than any one delivery job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Tariq and the other drivers to do the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pick something, anything, and start now. Not repairs necessarily, there's only room for so many. Tariq's good with people, he should look at the care homes.

say: Ten years means **no excuses**, for the government or for drivers.
He'd campaign for a **fair share** of machine profits and urge friends to start learning.
think: A decade lets him build the **repair business** properly and maybe hire someone.
By around **2039** he'd be 40, with ten years as the town's fixer.
do: Take **electronics** and then a **small business course**, both part-time.
Drop **evening takeaways** after two years once repairs cover rent.
Put spare money into **tools** rather than a newer car.
feel: **Good**, because this is the scenario where he's in charge.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd have learned how to learn, and that's worth more than any one delivery job.
fieldNote: Ben is the most **optimistic** driver: ten years turns his repair idea into a career.
He still expects repair work to be **automated eventually** but trusts his ability to learn.
He gives specific **advice for others**, steering a colleague, Tariq, toward care work.

steps.text: Take part-time electronics then small business courses
Run e-bike and robot repairs full-time once they cover rent
Buy repair tools instead of upgrading the car

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plans need a few years and that one gives me about three. What would help is a public fund for training and starting small businesses, so I don't have to borrow like my dad did. And a robot tax, so people who can't adapt still eat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what happens to towns like ours that depend on tourists. The tourists won't stop coming because of AGI, but the jobs serving them might stop needing us. A seaside town with no jobs is just a pretty place to be poor.

headlineQuote: A seaside town with no jobs is just a pretty place to be poor.
portrait: Ben is **27**, drives a second-hand hybrid for three apps and shares a flat with his cousin Omar.
He uses an **AI assistant daily** to plan hours and sort receipts for his tax.
He sees robot spread as a chance to become the town's **repair and robot** person.
He moves from **uneasy** to **anxious** with two years' notice, and is calm with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his plans need a few years and he'd get about three.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** for training and small businesses, so he needn't borrow.
A **robot tax** so people who can't adapt still eat.
